supplies needed to survive
in post-Great Destruction Tokyo.

Best suited for beginner Demon Busters.

・Gift Card (Newbie)
・Demon Depository Pass
 (30Days, Non-Trade)

*Use to acquire the above items.
*Cannot be traded or sold.

・2x Voucher (Depository Rental Ticket)

*Use to acquire the above items.
*Cannot be traded or sold.

Similarly to 'Remains of Tokyo' the element can be extracted. ※The raw material can be acquired using Deconstruction Catalyze: Extractors.

strings.アイルランド伝承の中で語り伝えられる妖精。\n名前は「妖精の恋人」の意味を持つ。:
A fairy told of in Irish legend.
Her name means "fairy lover".

A fairy who always seeks the love of human men and tempts them.
To the man Leanan Sidhe favors she looks very beautiful,
but others are said to be unable to even see her.

If the man refuses her love, she serves him like a slave;
if he accepts, she possesses him and grants him talent
in arts such as poetry and song.
In return his life force (sometimes said to be blood) is drained,
so she is sometimes seen as a kind of vampire.

The draining continues until Leanan Sidhe finds another man.

strings.アステカ神話に登場する暗闇と夜の魔神。\n\n太陽と争う星々の化身として、複数の:
A demon of darkness and night in Aztec mythology.

As incarnations of the stars that battle the sun, there are said to be
many "Tzitzimitl", collectively called the "Tzitzimimeh".
Solar eclipses were especially feared, as it was believed the Tzitzimimeh
would appear on earth and devour people.

When her granddaughter "Mayahuel" descended as a tree branch with the
cultural god "Quetzalcoatl" to give the earth the joy of liquor,
she flew into a rage at her granddaughter being taken, tearing the branch
apart and eating her, so jealous is her nature.

strings.フランスに伝わるドラゴンの一種。\n名前はviperaから派生している。vipe:
A kind of dragon told of in France.
Its name derives from vipera, meaning viper.

The Vouivre has the form of a giant snake
with bat-like wings and jewel eyes,
and is said to be female only.

It is said to live in deserted castles where treasure sleeps.

Usually it takes the form of a beautiful woman with a jewel
set in her forehead, which she removes when bathing.
Whoever holds this jewel is said to be able to use
all kinds of magic, so there was no end of
people trying to steal it.

The forehead jewel is also said to have been a garnet,
a ruby or a diamond.

strings.メソポタミア神話に登場する性愛、豊穣、戦いを司る女神。\nシュメール神話における:
A goddess of love, fertility and war in Mesopotamian myth.
Identified with Inanna of Sumerian myth,
she also symbolizes Venus and is called the Queen of Heaven.
A great goddess widely worshipped throughout the Orient,
she is said to have later become Anat of Canaanite myth,
Isis of Egyptian myth, and Aphrodite of Greek myth.

The kings of ancient Babylon needed a sacred marriage with Ishtar
to legitimize their rule, and in Ishtar's temples women called
sacred prostitutes are said to have given blessings in the goddess's
place through sexual rites.
Thus Ishtar was seen as protector of kingship and of prostitutes.

In "The Descent of Ishtar to the Underworld", when Ishtar descended
and was killed by Ereshkigal, mistress of death, love vanished from
the earth, all reproduction ceased, neither people nor animals were
born, and no crops grew.
Later, when her husband Dumuzi was taken to the underworld in her
place and Ishtar returned, the earth regained love and harvests.

While traveling, "Odin", "Loki" and "Hoenir" killed "Otr",

"Loki" stole a gold-producing ring from the dwarf "Andvari"

killed "Hreidmar", took it and fled to "Gnitaheidr",
and turned into a poison-breathing dragon to guard it

strings.古代ローマ神話における、運命の女神。\n古代における都市国家の守護神である彼女へ:
The goddess of fate in ancient Roman myth.
As a guardian of ancient city-states, she was worshipped widely outside Rome since long ago.
In the ancient Italian city of Praeneste she was worshipped as a goddess of prophecy,
and in Greek myth she is identified with Tyche, goddess of fortune.
In the Hellenistic era she was also identified with the Egyptian goddess Isis.
She is also said to have originally been a goddess of fertility.

She is mainly depicted holding a rudder that steers fate, standing on a sphere,
a symbol of instability.
She symbolizes unpredictable fate, instability and chance.
However, as a goddess who foretold children and victory in war, she had followers
from commoners to emperors, and in such cases was worshipped as a goddess of luck.

She is depicted with hair only in front (or all her hair tied forward).
If you pass her and chase after her, you can't grab her because she has no hair in back.
This means you must act at once to seize a chance.
Leonardo da Vinci spread this story, but it is said
he confused it with the tale of Kairos, Greek god of opportunity.

She is also often depicted blindfolded,
showing that she can't choose fate at will, and fate itself is unforeseeable.

She is said to be the origin of the English word "Fortune".
The Major Arcana tarot card "Wheel of Fortune" is also said to be based on her.
strings.古代ローマ神話に登場する女神。\n『ディアナ』、『ディアーナ』としての読み方でも:
A goddess of ancient Roman myth.
Also known by the readings "Diana" and "Diane".

Originally a goddess of trees said to bring fertility,
but through the influence of Greek myth, especially "Artemis",
her myths mainly concerned the moon, hunting and chastity.

As a moon goddess in particular, she is sometimes seen as a triple goddess:
"Luna" of the heavens, "Diana" of the earth and "Proserpina" of the underworld,
corresponding to the full, new and waning moon.

When Christianity spread in the Middle Ages she was seen as pagan,
and came to be treated as a goddess followed by witches.

In Japanese myth, she was born from the left eye of Izanagi
when he purified himself after returning from the land of Yomi.
One of the "Three Noble Children" with Tsukuyomi and Susano-o.

and the sun god, the deified sun.

She is generally said to be female, but when her brother Susano-o
visited Takamagahara to say farewell before going to the Root Land,
Amaterasu suspected he had come to seize it, and met him dressed as
a man: wearing the Yasakani beads and a war armguard, carrying a bow
and fifteen hundred arrows, her hair tied in a man's style.

strings.白娘子。\n中国の民間に伝わる物語『白蛇伝』に登場するヒロイン。\n白娘々（パイ:
Bai Suzhen.
The heroine of the Chinese folk tale "Legend of the White Snake".
Also called Bai Niangniang.

A white snake spirit that trained for a thousand years on the sacred
Mount Emei in Sichuan and mastered hermit arts.
She took the form of a beautiful woman in white to see the human world,
fell in love with a man named "Xu Xian", married him and had a child.

The monk "Fahai" of "Jinshan Temple" saw she was a monster
and imprisoned her beneath "Leifeng Pagoda".

Her maid "Xiaoqing" trained for eighteen years on Mount Emei to save her.
Becoming invincible, Xiaoqing burned Leifeng Pagoda and rescued her,
and she was reunited with her child.

In "Taiping Guangji: Record of the White Snake", she was depicted as an
evil woman who took the form of a beauty in white, seduced a young man
and drained his essence to kill him.
Over time she came to be treated as a good snake spirit, with love added to the tale.

strings.雪女郎。\n日本各地に伝わる、雪の夜に現れる女の妖怪。\nユキジョロウはとても美:
Yuki Jyorou.
A female yokai of snowy nights told of all over Japan.
Yuki Jyorou is said to be a very beautiful woman,
but there are many legends and names in each region, such as
Yuki-onna, Yuki-anesa, Yuki-banba, Yukifuri-baba and Tsurara-onna;
she may appear not only as a beautiful woman but as an old woman,
and there are one-legged legends such as Shikkenken.
She often appears with a child, and is sometimes linked to the Ubume.

Many have the nature of a mountain god, and while she is often told of
as a danger of snowy nights who freezes people to death, eats them,
drains their vitality or pushes them into ravines,
there are also many tales of her as a princess from the moon,
or vanishing like snow.

The Yuki-onna of Lafcadio Hearn's "Kwaidan"
is portrayed as a charming being with two faces:
she takes lives without hesitation, yet falls for a young man at first sight.

strings.１３４７年からヨーロッパで黒死病が大流行した。\n当時は有効な治療策がなく、死者:
From 1347, the Black Death swept through Europe.
There was no effective cure at the time, and the dead are estimated at 20 to 30 million.
It was also during the Hundred Years' War, and deaths from fighting never ceased.
It deeply impressed on people how fragile life is, and that high rank and
military honors are utterly powerless before death.

The art style called the Dance of Death began to appear around then.
The universality of death was a common theme of paintings, murals and prints,
with shared features such as dancing skeletons, skeletons playing instruments,
or skeletons leading dancing living people to the grave.
The living are shown from royalty to serfs, of every occupation.
It expresses the view that death, which comes suddenly one day,
unites all in nothingness regardless of rank or wealth.
